strengths: Addresses a genuine and important gap: existing 3D affordance grounding datasets are small, closed-vocabulary, and derived from the same limited asset source (PartNet/3D AffordanceNet), and the paper convincingly shows these limitations (Fig. 4: annotation mismatch, incomplete coverage, sparse resolution).

Substantial scale and diversity: 150K 3D object instances and 750K open-vocabulary query–heatmap pairs, roughly 5x larger than prior datasets and drawn from Objaverse/G-Objaverse with four diverse subsets, representing a meaningful resource for the community.

The Affogato-Engine pipeline (Gemma3 for query generation, Molmo for interaction-point prediction, SAM for mask decoding, followed by multi-view voting into 3D heatmaps) is a sensible, well-motivated use of foundation models for scalable annotation, and the multi-view aggregation addresses per-view inconsistency.

Unified treatment of 3D and 2D affordance grounding from the same source is novel and practically useful; the 2D heatmaps are projected consistently from 3D geometry, enabling aligned cross-modal supervision.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough: cross-dataset generalization (LASO), open-vocabulary cross-domain splits (Daily-Used ↔ Furnitures), zero-shot and fine-tuned 2D evaluation on AGD20K, partial-view analysis (Affogato-Partial), and qualitative results.

The paper is largely honest about limitations: human quality assessment (72.3% good / 12.3% ok / 15.4% not good), explicit failure-mode analysis (LLM misidentification, SAM edge bias, occlusion), test-split refinement, and a limitations discussion.

The Espresso models, while simple, are lightweight, use frozen pretrained encoders to preserve generalization, and the paper demonstrates that pretraining on Affogato improves downstream 2D performance (state-of-the-art on AGD20K-Full) and cross-domain robustness.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is a central concern for a dataset paper: ~28% of automatically generated query–heatmap pairs are rated below 'good', and only the 5K test split is manually refined. The bulk of the training data retains these imperfections, which could bias or limit models trained on it; the claim of 'high-quality affordance annotations' is therefore only partially supported.

The dataset-level 'diversity' (average pairwise KL divergence between heatmaps) and 'coverage' metrics are self-defined and will naturally favor the authors' multi-view aggregated annotations; they are not clearly established proxies for annotation correctness, so the quantitative comparison to LASO (Tab. 3d) is somewhat self-serving.

The Espresso architecture has limited technical novelty, being an adaptation of OOAL/standard mask-decoder designs with frozen CLIP and modality encoders; the paper is explicitly dataset-centric, but the model does not advance the state of the art on in-dataset LASO (Espresso-3D aIoU 0.178 vs. PointRefer 0.192), so its role is largely as a validation vehicle.

The 2D zero-shot comparison (Tab. 4a) pits Espresso-2D against general-purpose LLM/segmentation models (Molmo+SAM, LISA, M²SA) that are not affordance-specialized, which may overstate the advantage; the more informative comparison is Tab. 4b, where gains are real but smaller.

Data are derived entirely from synthetic Objaverse meshes with no real background or scene context; real-world transfer is only partially addressed (random background augmentation, 2D fine-tuning), and the paper acknowledges background information is absent, limiting claims about real-world applicability.

Some quantitative reporting is confusing: Tab. 2 shows counterintuitive MAE increases (acknowledged but only explained post-hoc), and combined/multi-part tables (e.g., Tab. 4a/4b) are dense; error bars or significance tests are absent throughout.

The apparent 2x baseline comparison in Tab. 2 and Tab. 3 mixes in-dataset and cross-dataset settings, and the 'coverage/diversity' argument would be stronger with independent verification or a correlation analysis against human quality judgments beyond the 5K test sample.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale affordance grounding dataset, Affogato, with 150K 3D object instances and 750K open-vocabulary query-heatmap pairs, substantially improving scale and diversity over prior datasets.

Provides an automated Affogato-Engine pipeline using Gemma3, Molmo, and SAM, with multi-view aggregation and a human-refined test split; the pipeline is described in detail and includes human quality assessment.

Integrates 3D and 2D affordance grounding and offers simple Espresso-3D/2D baselines with frozen foundation encoders; the 2D zero-shot and fine-tuned AGD20K results are strong, and cross-dataset generalization improvements are demonstrated.
Includes useful analyses of prior dataset limitations, failure modes, partial-view robustness, and implementation details, supporting reproducibility and transparency.
The dataset and benchmark target an important problem in embodied vision and could enable further research if annotation quality is validated more rigorously.
weaknesses: Annotation quality is validated only on a small sample (1K objects / 5K pairs); 15.4% of evaluated pairs were rated "not good," and only the test split is human-refined. The training split likely contains substantial label noise, yet the paper claims high-quality annotations without fully supporting that claim.

Potential circularity: annotations are generated by Gemma3/Molmo/SAM, and Espresso-2D pretrained on Affogato is compared against Molmo+SAM; gains may partly reflect distillation or multi-view aggregation rather than independent affordance learning.

3D results are modest in absolute terms (e.g., aloU 0.067 on Affogato, 0.182 cross-domain) and not uniformly better than baselines; no comparison to stronger 3D foundation models or human performance is provided.
The 2D benchmark is evaluated only on AGD20K, not on the proposed Affogato 2D test split, so the claimed joint 2D/3D benchmark is not fully validated.

Method novelty is limited: the pipeline combines off-the-shelf foundation models, and the Espresso architecture is a standard text-conditioned decoder; the contribution rests mainly on dataset scale and automation rather than new algorithmic insight.
The human evaluation lacks quantitative inter-annotator agreement, and there is no ablation on training with cleaned versus noisy annotations or on how query diversity/quality affects performance.
Diversity and coverage metrics may reward annotation spread without ensuring semantic correctness; MAE is acknowledged as unreliable but still included in comparisons.
Some claims, such as being the first to integrate 3D and 2D affordance grounding and producing high-quality annotations, are overstated relative to the presented evidence.

strengths: Scale and diversity of the Affogato dataset (150K 3D objects, 750K open-vocabulary query–heatmap pairs) substantially exceed prior 3D affordance datasets (e.g., 3D AffordanceNet's ~23K objects derived from a single source), directly addressing a genuine bottleneck in affordance grounding research.

The Affogato-Engine pipeline is well-motivated and sensibly engineered: VLM-generated open-vocabulary queries (Gemma3), point grounding (Molmo), mask generation (SAM), and multi-view voting aggregation to resolve per-view inconsistency. The human quality study (72.3% 'good', 12.3% 'ok') and the human-refined test split provide reasonable, if partial, quality control.

The paper provides concrete evidence that the dataset is useful: cross-dataset evaluation (Table 2) shows smaller generalization gaps when training on Affogato than on LASO, cross-domain generalization over non-overlapping object categories (Table 3) shows gains, and zero-shot transfer to an entirely unseen class (fox → 'pet'/'ride') is a compelling qualitative result.

2D transfer results on AGD20K are strong: a lightweight DINOv2+CLIP model pretrained on Affogato outperforms heavily parameterized LLM-based zero-shot methods (Molmo+SAM, LISA-7B, M²SA-7B) and reaches state-of-the-art when fine-tuned on AGD20K-Full.

The analysis of prior dataset limitations (annotation mismatch, incomplete heatmap coverage, insufficient data resolution, illustrated in Fig. 4) is informative and helps justify the new dataset's design.

Presentation is clear and well organized, with honest discussion of failure modes (Gemma3 misclassification, SAM edge bias, occlusion) and an explicit limitations statement (no background information, only contact points, no pose/force).

The Espresso baselines, despite being simple, are an appropriate reference point for a dataset paper and validate the dataset's utility across both 2D and 3D modalities with a shared architectural concept.
weaknesses: Ground-truth circularity is a substantive concern: the Affogato benchmark's 'ground truth' heatmaps are produced by the same Molmo+SAM pipeline that Espresso-2D is effectively trained on, so evaluation on Affogato may reward models that share the pipeline's inductive biases. Espresso-2D's zero-shot advantage on AGD20K is partly a distillation effect of the Molmo+SAM annotation engine, which the paper does not disentangle.

Only a small fraction of the data was human-validated (1K objects / 5K pairs), and even within this verified subset 15.4% were rated 'not good'; the remaining ~150K training annotations are unvalidated. The paper does not quantify how this label noise affects training or the reported evaluation numbers, nor does it report inter-annotator agreement or annotator qualifications for the 'domain experts'.

Architectural novelty is limited: the text-conditional heatmap decoder using text embeddings as queries follows standard transformer mask-decoder designs, and the 3D encoder is frozen PartField. This is acceptable for a dataset-centric contribution, but the framing as a modeling contribution ('simple yet effective baseline') overstates the methodological originality.

The diversity metric (average pairwise KL divergence between heatmaps of an object) conflates genuine functional diversity with annotation inconsistency; high diversity could equally reflect multi-view disagreement/noise. Coverage and diversity are reported without a human-anchored sanity check of what the values mean in practice.

Comparisons against prior datasets are not fully controlled: there is no matched-scale ablation isolating the effect of data quantity versus annotation quality, and no direct evaluation of whether Affogato pretraining improves performance on the original 3D AffordanceNet benchmark (only LASO is used, whose heatmaps are inherited from 3D AffordanceNet, so this is partly addressed but not explicitly separated).

The paper does not discuss data provenance/licensing of Objaverse assets or the distributional biases of web-crawled 3D meshes, and societal-impact considerations are largely absent; this matters for a dataset that is released publicly.

Some improvement claims rest on metrics with acknowledged caveats (e.g., counterintuitive MAE increases in Table 2), and the explanation (annotation-scale sensitivity) is plausible but not empirically verified, e.g., by normalizing heatmap magnitudes and re-running the comparison.

The 'largest 3D affordance grounding dataset' claim rests on class/affordance counts obtained via word-frequency thresholds (>450 classes, >350 affordances), which is a heuristic definition of vocabulary breadth that could inflate the reported diversity relative to prior datasets using curated taxonomies.

strengths: Large-scale, open-vocabulary resource: Affogato-750K provides 750K query–heatmap annotations over 150K Objaverse 3D assets with >450 object classes and >350 affordance categories (Table 1), an order-of-magnitude increase over LASO (1,871 objects / 42K questions) and substantially broader coverage than existing 3D and 2D affordance datasets.

The automated annotation pipeline (Gemma3 query generation → Molmo point prediction → MobileSAM masks → multi-view voting into 3D heatmaps) is clearly described, uses attributed off-the-shelf foundation models, and is a practical recipe that is explicitly argued to be transferable to other 3D repositories.

Evidence for dataset utility is unusually thorough for a dataset paper: consistent pretraining gains on LASO unseen split across three different architectures (OpenAD +0.9 aIoU, PointRefer +4.0, Espresso-3D +2.1), improvements on AGD20K zero-shot and fully supervised 2D settings, a monotonic data-scale ablation (Table A3), a cross-domain asymmetry study (Table A4), and a resolution ablation (Table A2).

Credibility of the annotation is probed rather than asserted: 5K human-verified pairs (84.8% success), a per-stage failure-mode breakdown (Fig. 4), a qualitative pipeline-vs-human comparison (Fig. A2), and a held-out-category filtering experiment (Table 5) that explicitly rules out the trivial explanation that gains come from pretraining categories that benchmarks hold out.

Reproducibility is well supported: model identifiers/checkpoints (google/gemma-3-4b-it, allenai/Molmo-7B-D-0924, MobileSAM), image sampling strategy, compute budget, training hyperparameters, losses, and fine-tuning protocols for both 3D and 2D are given in the appendix.

The Espresso models are a sensible design choice for the stated goal (isolating the dataset's contribution via a symmetric 2D/3D architecture), and the paper honestly frames them as 'simple yet effective' baselines rather than a novel-architecture claim.
Writing and organization are clear; limitations (no background in the source assets, no temporal/force information) are stated explicitly and used to motivate concrete future work.
weaknesses: The ground truth is model-generated, yet the paper never quantifies agreement between the pipeline and independent human annotation beyond a single qualitative figure (Fig. A2) and a self-reported 84.8% 'success' rate whose rubric and aggregation are not defined. A quantitative IoU/aIoU comparison against human masks on 3DAffordanceNet meshes (the data is already available, as Fig. A2 shows) would substantially strengthen the central claim that the pipeline is 'a reliable substitute for manual annotation'.

Circularity risk is only partially addressed. Espresso is trained on annotations produced by Molmo+MobileSAM, and in-domain Affogato-750K results (Table 3, All→All, 13.6 aIoU) may partly reflect learning to reproduce Molmo/SAM biases rather than affordance structure. The cross-domain and held-out-filter analyses mitigate but do not eliminate this; an evaluation against an independently annotated, non-Molmo-derived benchmark at scale would help.

Improvement magnitudes on LASO are modest in absolute terms (e.g., Espresso-3D +1.5 seen / +2.1 unseen aIoU; OpenAD +0.9 unseen), and PointRefer degrades on the seen split with Affogato pretraining (20.2 vs. 20.8). The text's language of 'substantial and consistent gains' and 'largest gains' overstates the effect size; the consistency across methods is the real evidence, not the magnitude.

The synthetic-to-real generalization result (Fig. 7, Open X-Embodiment) is presented only qualitatively. No metric, no baseline, and no quantitative comparison is reported for the one experiment that most directly probes transfer to real embodied settings — a notable gap given how strongly the conclusion leans on this point.

The dataset is heavily imbalanced: Daily-Used contains 121,799 of 150,104 instances (~81%), while Transportation, Furniture, and Electronics have 7,937–11,609. This skew is acknowledged for the cross-domain asymmetry, but its effect on the learned affordance distribution and on the reported category-diversity claims is not analyzed.

The reported '>450 classes' and '>350 affordances' are Gemma3 predictions filtered by frequency (>10 and >100), not a human-verified taxonomy. Diversity/coverage numbers (Fig. 3d, Table 3d) are self-defined metrics computed against a single baseline (LASO), so the 'significantly more diverse than any existing dataset' claim is weaker than presented.

The 2D split is obtained by projecting 3D heatmaps onto rendered views, yielding one selected view per object (150,101 images for 150,104 objects) with no background and no real imagery. This limits the 2D data's diversity in appearance and viewpoint; the paper relies on background augmentation (Table A1) and Open X-Embodiment transfer to compensate, but the 2D split's own domain coverage remains narrow.

Minor issues: the manuscript refers to 'Table 3d' where the diversity metrics appear in Fig. 3(d); the human-verification protocol does not report annotator count per pair, inter-annotator agreement, or how many of the 5K pairs were re-annotated; and Section A (dataset link) is empty in the reviewed version, leaving release/ licensing terms (Objaverse-derived assets) unaddressed.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and well-argued bottleneck in visual affordance grounding—data scarcity and closed-vocabulary annotation—and addresses it with a concrete, scalable solution. Affogato-750K is substantially larger and more diverse than existing datasets (>450 object classes, >350 affordance classes, 750K annotations over 150K objects vs. 23–304 classes in prior work), which is a meaningful contribution to the community.

The automated annotation pipeline is thoughtfully designed: it chains complementary foundation models (Gemma3 for query generation, Molmo for point grounding, MobileSAM for masks) and crucially aggregates per-view predictions into 3D heatmaps via multi-view voting, which is a principled way to suppress per-view errors. Design choices such as CoT prompting and smallest-mask selection are justified both qualitatively (Fig. 8) and by the failure analysis.

The empirical validation is thorough and convincing. Pretraining on Affogato-750K yields consistent improvements on LASO (seen and unseen), AGD20K, and both Espresso models as well as prior methods (OpenAD, PointRefer, AffordanceNet), with the largest gains on unseen object/affordance combinations, supporting the claim of broadly transferable supervision.

The paper includes strong controls that strengthen the scientific case: (i) held-out category filtering to rule out that gains come from benchmark overlap, (ii) pretraining-data-scale analysis showing monotonic improvement, (iii) cross-domain asymmetry analysis, (iv) resolution ablation, and (v) zero-shot transfer to real-world Open X-Embodiment robot scenes. These go beyond typical dataset papers.

Human validation (84.8% success) with a curated, held-out 5K test split, plus an explicit breakdown of failure modes and their originating pipeline stages, gives a credible and honest picture of annotation quality.

Clarity and reproducibility are good: the pipeline is clearly diagrammed (Fig. 2, Fig. A5), implementation details (models, checkpoints, GPUs, hyperparameters, training iterations) are provided in the appendix, and limitations are discussed explicitly.
weaknesses: The dataset is built exclusively from Objaverse synthetic renders without background context. Although background augmentation and real-world transfer experiments partially mitigate this, the synthetic-to-real domain gap and the quality/realism limitations of Objaverse assets remain a genuine constraint on downstream applicability, as the authors acknowledge.

The Espresso models are largely adaptations of prior architectures (PointRefer for 3D, OOAL for 2D) rather than new designs, so the algorithmic novelty is modest. This is defensible given the stated goal of isolating dataset contribution, but it means the paper's value rests primarily on the dataset and pipeline.

The automatic annotations are ~85% correct, and the paper does not fully characterize how residual label noise propagates into model training (the test split is cleaned, but the training split is not). Affordance ground truth is inherently ambiguous (the paper itself shows cases with multiple plausible regions), and heatmap supervision is only one possible formulation.
Some baselines required re-training by the authors (e.g., OpenAD on LASO) due to unavailable official results, which introduces a risk of implementation mismatch that is not fully quantified.

The human-verified test split is relatively small (5K) and drawn from the same source distribution as training, so it may not fully stress-test generalization to genuinely novel object/affordance categories.

strengths: Affogato-750K is genuinely large and diverse: 750K open-vocabulary annotations over 150K 3D assets with >350 object/affordance classes, far beyond the ~23 classes of prior 3D datasets (Table 1). This directly targets a real, well-motivated data bottleneck in affordance grounding.

The automated annotation pipeline is sensible and well-engineered, chaining Gemma3 (query generation with CoT prompting), Molmo (interaction-point prediction), and MobileSAM (mask generation) with multi-view voting for 3D aggregation and smallest-mask selection. Design choices are motivated and ablated (Figs. 2, 8).

Evaluation is broad and uses external benchmarks: 3D on LASO (seen/unseen), 2D on AGD20K (zero-shot and supervised), plus synthetic-to-real transfer on Open X-Embodiment (Fig. 7). Gains from Affogato-750K pretraining are demonstrated across multiple architectures (OpenAD, PointRefer, Espresso).

The analysis is unusually thorough for a dataset paper: held-out category filtering to rule out train/test overlap (Table 5), pretraining-data scale analysis (Table A3), cross-domain asymmetry decomposition (Table A4), and explicit enumeration of failure modes (Fig. 4, Sec. C.1).

A human-verified 5K test split and 84.8% human validation give at least partial evidence of annotation reliability, and the appendix provides reproducible details (specific checkpoints, hyperparameters, and compute).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The pipeline is essentially a composition of off-the-shelf foundation models, and Espresso-3D/2D are adapted from PointRefer/OOAL; the paper itself calls them 'minimal' and presents them as a unified baseline. The algorithmic contribution is thin, so the case rests almost entirely on the dataset.

Data quality is not fully validated. Only 84.8% of sampled annotations pass human validation, with dominant failure modes being wrong interaction points (34.9%) and incorrect queries (36.8% of failures); these errors are retained in the 750K training set, and their downstream effect on the reported gains is never quantified. The human-validation protocol is under-specified: it is unclear how semantic relevance, spatial accuracy, and coverage are combined into a binary 'success', and no inter-annotator agreement is reported.

Potential circularity. The 5K test split is derived from the same pipeline and then human re-annotated, so the in-domain result on Affogato-750K (Table 3) partly measures agreement with the pipeline's own output distribution. External benchmarks partially mitigate this, but the 3D LASO gains for Espresso-3D are modest (+1.5 aIoU seen, +2.1 unseen), and PointRefer actually degrades on LASO seen.

Absolute performance is low (13.6 aIoU in-domain on Affogato-750K; 2.8–18.2 aIoU in cross-domain), and the strong cross-domain asymmetry (Table 3) hints at uneven internal consistency of the dataset. The paper does not disentangle how much of this reflects genuine task difficulty versus annotation noise/inconsistency.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence ('eliminating costly manual annotation', 'broadly transferable supervision'), and the 2D comparison is not apples-to-apples: Espresso-2D zero-shot is compared against baselines trained only on AGD20K, so the gap largely reflects a pretraining-data-scale advantage rather than a method advantage (Table 4a).

The source subset selection (Daily-Used, Furnitures, Transportations, Electronics) is somewhat arbitrary, and the use of only 25 fixed-elevation views is acknowledged to cause 10.5% of failures, further limiting coverage.
